::: frame
### What is statistics?

- Statistics is the science of [*learning from data*]{style="color: magenta"}. It uses the theory of probability to make inferences about populations or processes using data

- For example, we would like to know the mean of a characteristic of a set of elements of a population

- But we can't observe or measure each one because there are too many elements or not all are available.
:::

::: frame
### Examples

- Mean blood pressure of 40 year old pregnant females.

- Mean lifetime of 60-watt bulbs being made at the G.E. plant in Cleveland.

- Mean potency of an antibiotic after storage for 20 months on store shelves.
:::

::: frame
### Statistics is Useful in

- Data collection

  - Sample survey design

  - Experimental design

- Drawing conclusion from data

  - Descriptive methods - summarization and presentation of data

  - Statistical inference - make statements about an entire population based on a sample
:::

::: frame
### Population versus Sample

Since we can't obtain the average exactly, we do the next best thing

- approximate it by finding the average for a [*selected subset*]{style="color: magenta"} of the elements

- we do a statistical study to estimate the population mean

- usually, there are many objectives of a [*statistical study*]{style="color: magenta"}, than just estimating the mean of the population.
:::

::: frame
### Steps in a Statistical Study

- [Collecting data]{style="color: magenta"} - by making observations or taking measurements on some sample or process of interest, possibly as a part of a statistically designed experiment or a survey.

- [Summarizing the data]{style="color: magenta"} - using statistical summary methods (calculating means or constructing a histogram, for example).

- [Analyzing the data and making inferences]{style="color: magenta"} - using models and statistical methods for drawing conclusions about the situation being considered.
:::

::: frame
### Terminology and definitions

- [Population]{style="color: magenta"} - The set of all objects (or measurements) of interest; they are called elements of the population.

- [Sample]{style="color: magenta"} - Any subset of elements from a population.

- A statistical study is made using a sample obtained from a population.

- Sample represents the population.
:::

::: frame
### How to Select a Sample?

Theoretically we can get a random sample of $n$ elements by

- making n draws, one at a time

- on each draw, each remaining element in the population is [equally likely]{style="color: magenta"} to be the one drawn.

Practically we can seldom satisfy the theoretical requirements, so we do the best we can to introduce randomness into our sample selection process.
:::

::: frame
### How to Select a Sample? (continued)

- Can the result of a statistical study of population mean (average) be far away from the true mean? - sure, sometimes. A statistical study provides evidence. It doesn't prove anything\

- A random sample selected using the method described earlier ensures that each sample of size $n$ drawn from a population has the same chance of being selected

- Methods that ensure this property are called [simple random sampling]{style="color: magenta"}

- We shall use a method for selecting a simple random sample from a population in a one of our labs using random digit tables
:::

::: frame
### Some Important Definitions

- [Data value:]{style="color: magenta"} measurement

- [Observation:]{style="color: magenta"} Row of data values

- [Variable:]{style="color: magenta"} Set of data values for the same type of measurement

- [Data set:]{style="color: magenta"} The entire collection of data values
:::

::: frame

::: frame
### Data Description

- [Two broad applications of Statistics]{style="color: magenta"}\

  - descriptive statistics

  - inferential statistics

- When measurements from an entire population is available to us data description will be a major objective.

- In this case, methods for organizing, summarizing, and describing data are needed.

- Good descriptive statistics enable us to make sense of the data by reducing large amounts of data to a few summary measures and graphical displays.
:::

::: frame
### Data Description - cont.

- When only a random sample is available from a large population (or a process), inferential statistics becomes the major focus.

- However, even in this case, descriptive statistics of the sample data is still important as they can be used to draw conclusions about the population from which the sample was taken.

- Data descriptions are of two types:\

  - graphical methods

  - numerical summaries
:::

::: frame
### Graphical Methods

- Bar Chart

- Histogram

- Stem-and-Leaf plot

- Time Series plot

- Boxplot

- Normal Probability Plot
:::

::: frame
### Numerical Summaries

- Measures of Center or Location

  - Mode

  - Median

  - Mean

- Measures of Variability or Spread

  - Range

  - Percentile (Quantile, Quartile)

  - Interquartile Range

  - Variance

  - Standard Deviation

  - Coefficient of Variation
:::

::: frame
### Histograms

- To plot a histogram, a [*frequency table*]{style="color: magenta"} must first be constructed

- The range of the data is divided into [*class intervals*]{style="color: magenta"} or [*bins*]{style="color: magenta"}

- The number of such intervals is determined by the end-points of the intervals [*number of observations*]{style="color: magenta"} in the data set

- The larger the number of observations the more the number of class intervals we may use

- Divide the range of data values by the number of class intervals to determine an approximate [*class width*]{style="color: magenta"}
:::

::: frame
### Weight gains of chicks fed an antibiotic - Data

An animal scientist is carrying out an experiment to investigate whether adding an antibiotic to the diet of chicks will promote growth over the standard diet without the antibiotic. The scientist determines that 100 chicks will provide sufficient information to validate the results of the experiment. From previous research studies, the average weight gain of chicks fed the standard diet over an 8-week period is 3.9 grams. The scientist wants to compare the weight gain of the chicks in the study to the standard value of 3.9 grams. The weight gains for the 100 chicks are recorded the the table shown on the next slide.
:::

::: frame

::: frame
### Creating a Histogram

- It was decided to have 10 class intervals

- Since the range is $4.9-3.6=1.3$, a class interval width of $1.3/10  \approx .1$ was used

- The end-points of the intervals are incremented by one-half the unit of measurement (i.e., .05 gram, here)

- This is so that no observation falls on any end-point

- Since the smallest observation is 3.6 we start with the interval $3.55-3.65$

- Once the class intervals have been determined observations in the data set falling into each of these classes are tallied
:::

### Stem-and-Leaf Plots

- These are useful as an alternative to histograms or frequency tables.

- The idea is to substitute digits for frequency counts used in constructing histograms and thereby convey more information.

- Its profile is much like that of a histogram but it shows the numerical values of all observations.

- To construct a stem-and-leaf diagram, group each data value into two parts:

  - a set of [leading digits]{style="color: magenta"}, and

  - a set of [trailing digits]{style="color: magenta"}.
:::

::: frame
### Stem-and-Leaf Plots (continued)

- First write down, to the left of a vertical line, all possible values of the leading digits, in increasing order.

- Then we represent each data value by writing its trailing digits in the appropriate row to the right of the line.

- The column of digits on the left of the vertical line represents the [stem]{style="color: magenta"} and the digits on the right the [leaves]{style="color: magenta"} of the stem-and-leaf plot.

- Thus each data value can be reconstructed by combining its stem part and its leaf part.

- The leaves in each stem are usually written successively (and usually contiguously) in the increasing order of magnitude.
:::

:::: frame
### Stem-and-Leaf Plots (continued)

In those cases where the data values may not be adequately represented by just taking the last digits as leaves the data values must be appropriately rounded before a stem-and-leaf diagram can be constructed.\
**Example**\
Below are the measured manganese content (in points or .01%'s) for 20 heats of 1045 steel)

::: center
  ---- ---- ---- ---- ---- ---- ---- ----
    74   79   77   81   68   79   81   76
    81   80   80   78   88   83   79   91
    79   75   74   73                
  ---- ---- ---- ---- ---- ---- ---- ----
:::
::::

:::: frame
### Stem-and-Leaf Plots: Example

A stem and leaf diagram for these data is:\

::: center
  --- ----------
      
    6 8
    7 344
    7 56789999
    8 001113

    9 1
  --- ----------
:::
::::

::: frame
### Stem-and-Leaf Plots (continued)

- Some sets of observations have a very narrow range that the stem and leaf has only 2 or 3 stems.

- Such a plot is not useful for studying the distribution of the data.

- One solution is to attempt to increase the number of stems, by dividing the data into subgroups within each original stems i.e., to use each stem value twice or more.
:::

::: frame
### Stem-and-Leaf Plots: Example

- As an example, consider the following data of height in inches of students in a statistics class.

- The simplest stem-and-leaf plot is:

  ::: center
    --- ----------------------------
    5   47
    6   02333444555556666677777889
    7   00112223
    --- ----------------------------
  :::

- Obviously, this does not represent a satisfactory visual display of the distribution of the data.
:::

::: frame

- The following stem-and-leaf plot is the result:

      6a 02333444
      6b 555556666677777889
      7a 00112223

:::

### Quantiles and Percentiles

- The $80^{\rm th}$ [percentile]{style="color: magenta"} is a data value such that approximately 80% of the data values in the data set are less, and approximately 20% are larger, than that value.

- For a theoretical distribution (e.g. normal distribution) the .8 [quantile]{style="color: magenta"} is a value such that 80% of the probability mass of the distribution lies to the left and 20% lies to the right of the value of the quantile.

- For an empirical distribution (i.e., the distribution of a data set) we need another definition. Suppose we have 10 values in a dataset: $52, 63, 67, 71, 75, 76, 76, 82, 87, 94$
:::

::: frame
### Quantiles and Percentiles

- What is the 80th percentile? i.e., what value is such that approximately 80% are less and 20% are greater?

- Since there are 10 values, need to find a number such that 8 values are less, and 2 values greater than that number.

- There isn't a value in the data set that satisfies both conditions.

- A number half way between 82 and 87, i.e., 84.5, might be reasonably chosen as the $80^{\rm th}$ percentile.

- It satisfies the definition approximately.
:::

::: frame
### Quantiles and Percentiles

- A definition that will give unambiguous percentiles for any set of data is needed.

- Let $p\ (0 < p < 100)$ denote the desired percentile, $n$ the number of data values, and let $y_{(1)}, y_{(2)}, \ldots y_{(n)}$ denote the ordered observations so that $$y_{(1)} \le y_{(2)} \le \ldots  \le y_{(n)}$$
:::

::: frame
### Definition: Percentiles and Quantiles

- If $p$ is one of the numbers $100(i-.5)/n$ then $y_{(i)}$ is the $p^{\rm th}$ [percentile]{style="color: magenta"}, for i = 1, 2, 3, \..., n-1 or n.

- If $p$ is between $100(0.5/n)$ and $100(n-.5)/n$, and $p$ is not one of the numbers $100(i-.5)/n$ then the percentile is obtained by linear interpolation between the two percentiles that bracket $p$.

- `Quantiles` are a generalization of percentiles. The $p^{\rm th}$ quantile of a dataset is the $100p^{\rm th}$ percentile.
:::

::: frame
### Quantiles and Percentiles

Thus the $p^{\rm th}$ [quantile]{style="color: magenta"} of the dataset $y_{(1)}, y_{(2)}, \ldots y_{(n)}$ is obtained as follows:

1.  If $p$ is one of the numbers $(i-.5)/n$ then $y_{(i)}$ is the $p^{\rm th}$ quantile, for i = 1, 2, 3, \..., n-1 or n.

2.  If $p$ is between $(0.5/n)$ and $(n-.5)/n$, and $p$ is not one of the numbers $(i-.5)/n$ then the quantile is obtained by linear interpolation between the two quantiles that bracket p.

3.  The $p_i^{\rm th}$ quantile of a dataset is denoted by $Q(p_i)$
:::

:::: frame
### Quantiles and Percentiles: Example

Suppose we have a dataset consisting of the 10 observations: $9.614,  9.614,  10.688,  7.583,  8.572,  8.527,  8.577,  9.471,
9.165,  9.011$ The following table shows the ordered data values as the specified [quantiles]{style="color: magenta"}:

::: center
   $i$   $p_i=(i-.5)/10$   $Q(p_i)$
  ----- ----------------- ----------
    1         0.05          7.583
    2         0.15          8.527
    3         0.25          8.572
    4         0.35          8.577
    5         0.45          9.011
    6         0.55          9.165
    7         0.65          9.471
    8         0.75          9.614
    9         0.85          9.614
   10         0.95          10.688
:::
::::

::: frame
### Quantiles by Linear Interpolation

- $Q(p)$ for values of $p = (i-.5)/n$ correspond to the ordered observations for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$. For example $Q(.55)=9.165$.

- How is, say, $Q(.525)$ determined? This is obtained by linear interpolation between the two quantiles that bracket $.525$ i.e, $Q(.45)$ and $Q(.55)$.

- For a $p$ such that $p_i < p < p_{i+1},\ Q(p)$ is computed as the weighted average $Q(p) = (1-f)Q(p_i) + fQ(p_{i+1})$ where $f =(p-p_i)/(p_{i+1}-p_i) = n(p-p_i)$
:::

::: frame
### Quantiles by Linear Interpolation: Example

- Suppose $n = 10$ and one needs to compute $Q(.525)$.

- Since $.45 < p < .55, \ f = 10 (.525 - .45)  = .75$.

- Thus $Q(.525)=.25Q(.45) +
  .75Q(.55)$.

- In the above example, therefore $$Q(.525)= .25(9.011)+.75(9.165)=9.1265$$
:::

::: frame
### Box Plots (Tukey, 1977)

The boxplot is a summary display of a set of data, that is useful for studying the shape of the distribution including its symmetry or asymmetry around the central location, based on the quantiles $Q_1,\ M$, and $Q_3$ as defined below:

- Upper Quartile = $75^{ th} { percentile} =Q(.75)=Q_3$

- Median = $50^{ th} { percentile} =Q(.50)=M$

- Lower Quartile = $25^{ th} {percentile} =Q(.25)= Q_1$

- Interquartile Range (IQR) =\
  Upper Quartile - Lower Quartile =$Q_3- Q_1$
:::

::: frame
### Box Plots (continued)

The following quantities also need to be computed for constructing a box plot:

- Upper Fence = $Q_3 + 1.5$ IQR.

- Lower Fence = $Q_1 - 1.5$ IQR.

- Upper Adjacent Value: the largest observation below the upper fence

- Lower Adjacent Value: the smallest observation above the lower fence

- Outside Values: Observations that fall outside adjacent values.
:::

### Normal Probability Plot

- Consider a sample $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ of size $n$.

- The data are first ordered in increasing order of magnitude.

- Then a value $p$ is assigned to each data value using the formula $p = (i -
  0.5)/n$.

- Thus the ordered data values will be the $p_i^{\rm th}$ quantile $Q(p_i)$ for $i=1,2,\ldots,n.$

- Example: Quantiles for a data set with $n = 18$
:::

::: frame
### Normal Probability Plot:Example

- The quantile of the standard normal distribution, $z_p$, corresponding to each $p$ value, is then computed using the table of Normal percentiles (i.e. the $z$-table).

- The Normal Probability plot is the plot of the quantiles $Q(p)$ of the data vs. $z_p$, the corresponding standard normal quantiles.

- Thus this plot is also called the quantile-quantile plot or the Q-Q plot, in general.
:::

### Normal Probability Plot (continued)

- If the data is a random sample from a normal population the plotted points will lie approximately in a [straight-line]{style="color: magenta"}.

- [Departures]{style="color: magenta"} from a straight-line may indicate that the population distribution is different from a Normal distribution.

- Specific types of departures can be used to identify how the population distribution differs from a Normal distribution.

- The following pages contains normal robability plots of computer generated data from populations that resemble distributions that are as described.

::: frame
### Sample Statistics vs. Parameters

- A [parameter]{style="color: magenta"} is a descriptive statistic of a population.

- A [sample statistic]{style="color: magenta"} is a descriptive statistic of a sample.

- Take a [census]{style="color: magenta"} of a population recording values of a variable as $x_1, x_2,\ldots,x_N$, where $N$ is the population size, then

  - Population mean, $\mu=\frac{\textstyle\sum x}{N}$

  - Population variance, $\sigma^2=\frac{\textstyle\sum (x-\mu)^2}{N}$

  - Population standard deviation, $\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}$
:::

::: frame
### Sample Statistics vs. Parameters

- Since censuses cannot be taken for every population we wish to study, parameters cannot be exactly calculated and thus are usually unknown.

- Instead, a [random sample]{style="color: magenta"} of a population is taken recording values of a variable as $x_1, x_2,\ldots,x_n$, where $n$ is the sample size, then

  - sample mean (average, arithmetic mean), $\bar{x}= \frac{\textstyle \sum x}{n}$

  - sample variance, $s^2=\frac{\textstyle \sum (x-\bar{x})^2}{n-1}$

  - sample standard deviation, $s=\sqrt{s^2}$
:::

::: frame
### Sample Statistics vs. Parameters

- $\mu$, $\sigma^2$, and $\sigma$ are [parameters]{style="color: magenta"}.

- $\bar{x}$, $s^2$, and $s$ are [sample statistics]{style="color: magenta"}.
:::

:::: frame
### Sample Statistics vs. Parameters: Example

Calculate the sample mean, variance, and standard deviation for data: 2, 3, 3, 4, 3.

::: center
  $i$             $x$            $x^2$
  ----- ------------- ----------------
  1                 2                4
  2                 3                9
  3                 3                9
  4                 4               16
  5                 3                9
          $\sum x=15$   $\sum x^2= 47$
:::
::::

::: frame
### Sample Statistics vs. Parameters

Compute sample variance $s^2$ and sample standard deviation $s$. $$\begin{eqnarray*}
s^2 & = &\frac{\textstyle\sum x^2 - \frac{(\textstyle\sum
x)^2}{n}}{n-1}=\frac{47-\frac{(15)^2}{5}}{5-1}=2/4=0.5\\[.1in]
 s & = & \sqrt{(s^2)}=\sqrt{0.5}=0.71
\end{eqnarray*}$$
:::

::: frame
### Problems with the Variance and Standard Deviation

- The units of the variance are squared

- The standard deviation has the same units as the data

- Both $s$ and $s^2$ are absolute measures of variation, and many times the $s$ and $s^2$ cannot be compared for two different variables
:::

:::: frame
### Problems with the Variance and Standard Deviation - Example

- We would like to compare the standard deviation of auto speeds on I-80 with the German Autobahn, but speeds on I-80 are in MPH while speeds on the Autobahn are in km per hour.

::: center
               I-80   Autobahn
  ----------- ------ ----------
  $s^2$        144      625
  $\bar{x}$     63      120
:::
::::

::: frame
### Coefficient of Variation

- It is a relative measure of variability.

- [Coefficient of Variation:]{style="color: magenta"} $\frac{s}{\bar{x}}\times 100$
:::

:::: frame
### Coefficient of Variation - Example

::: center
                                    I-80    Autobahn
  ------------------------------- -------- ----------
  $s^2$                             144       625
  $\bar{x}$                          63       120
  $\frac{s}{\bar{x}}\times 100$    $19\%$    $20\%$
:::
::::

::: frame
### Numerical Summary Measures

- The sample mean and the sample median are examples of [numerical descriptive measures]{style="color: magenta"} of the [central tendency]{style="color: magenta"} of a sample and describes the center or location around which the data are distributed.

- The sample variance and standard deviation are examples of [numerical descriptive measures]{style="color: magenta"} of the [variability]{style="color: magenta"} or the [spread]{style="color: magenta"} of the sample around the center.

- These numerical descriptive measures are used both to describe a population, if the entire population of measurements is available, (e.g., census) or, to draw inferences about a population from the statistics calculated on a random sample drawn from the population.
:::

::: frame
### Other Numerical Summary Measures - Median

[Median:]{style="color: magenta"} Value at which $50\%$ of the observations are above and $50\%$ below.\
Computation of the sample median from a sample of size n:

- Arrange observations in ascending order

- The value of the $\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)^{th}$ ordered observation is the median

What is the median of $2,4,6,8,10$?\
What is the median of $2,4,6,10$?\
Location or spread?
:::

::: frame
### Other Numerical Summary Measures - Mode

[Mode:]{style="color: magenta"} Value which appears the most frequently.\
What is the mode?

- We count beetles on 12 plants, and 6 of them do not have any, but the other 6 has $3,2,6,1,5,6$.

- We count beetles on 12 plants, and 4 of them do not have any, 4 of them have 2 and 4 of them have 5.

Location or spread?
:::

::: frame
### Which measure of location should be used?

- When the data are symmetric?

- When data are skewed? Which means that there are some very large or very small values?
:::
